Bernat Martorell.who: The leading painter in Barcelona in his day, making altarpieces for churches and guilds.
Bernat Martorell.goodAt: Rich gold backgrounds, decorative detail and clear storytelling.

El Greco.from: Born in Crete, trained in Venice and Rome, settled in Toledo, Spain
El Greco.who: Born Doménikos Theotokópoulos; 'El Greco' just means 'the Greek'. He was largely forgotten after his death, then rediscovered by modern artists.
El Greco.goodAt: Stretched, flame-like figures, intense spiritual feeling and daring colour.

Diego Velázquez.who: Court painter to King Philip IV in Madrid for most of his career. His Las Meninas is one of the most studied paintings in the world.
Diego Velázquez.goodAt: Realism, light and loose brushwork that looks perfect from a distance. Manet called him 'the painter of painters'.

Francisco de Zurbarán.who: He painted mostly for monasteries and convents during Spain's Golden Age.
Francisco de Zurbarán.goodAt: Stillness, strong single light sources and painting white cloth so it feels touchable.

Rembrandt van Rijn.from: Leiden, worked in Amsterdam, the Netherlands
Rembrandt van Rijn.who: The most famous painter of the Dutch Golden Age. He painted around 40 self-portraits across his life, from confident youth to old age and debt.
Rembrandt van Rijn.goodAt: Light and shadow, and showing what people are thinking.

Jean-Siméon Chardin.who: He spent his career painting still lifes and quiet household scenes while grand history painting was the fashion.
Jean-Siméon Chardin.goodAt: Texture, calm, and making ordinary objects feel important.

Francisco de Goya.from: Aragon, Spain; died in exile in Bordeaux
Francisco de Goya.who: Court painter to the Spanish kings who also made some of the darkest art ever: his Disasters of War prints and the Black Paintings on the walls of his house.
Francisco de Goya.goodAt: Range. He could be playful, flattering, savage or terrifying, and he used art to criticise power.

J. M. W. Turner.who: A barber's son who entered the Royal Academy at 14. Britain's biggest art prize, the Turner Prize, is named after him.
J. M. W. Turner.goodAt: Light, weather and atmosphere. His late paintings are almost abstract.

Camille Corot.who: A landscape painter who worked outdoors in Italy and France and encouraged younger artists, including Pissarro and Morisot.
Camille Corot.goodAt: Soft, silvery light and calm, a bridge between classical painting and Impressionism.

Gustave Courbet.who: Leader of the Realist movement. He joined the Paris Commune in 1871, was jailed, and died in exile in Switzerland.
Gustave Courbet.goodAt: Painting ordinary people honestly and at full size, the way only kings and saints had been painted before.

Rosa Bonheur.who: The most famous woman painter of the nineteenth century. Her huge Horse Fair made her name in Europe and America.
Rosa Bonheur.goodAt: Animals, studied with real anatomical precision.

Édouard Manet.who: His paintings Olympia and Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe caused public scandals. Younger painters saw him as their leader, though he never showed with the Impressionists.
Édouard Manet.goodAt: Bold modern subjects, flat strong contrasts and challenging how a painting should look.

James McNeill Whistler.from: Born in Massachusetts, worked in Paris and London
James McNeill Whistler.who: Best known for the portrait usually called 'Whistler's Mother'. He sued the critic John Ruskin for libel and won one farthing in damages.
James McNeill Whistler.goodAt: Mood and harmony. He wanted painting to work like music.

Edgar Degas.who: A founder of the Impressionist exhibitions, though he called himself a realist. Famous for ballet dancers, which he painted hundreds of times.
Edgar Degas.goodAt: Movement, unusual angles and pastel. His compositions often look like snapshots.

Paul Cézanne.who: Mostly ignored for years, then hugely influential. Both Picasso and Matisse are said to have called him 'the father of us all'.
Paul Cézanne.goodAt: Structure. He built pictures from blocks of colour and paved the way for Cubism.

Claude Monet.from: Paris and Le Havre; later Giverny, France
Claude Monet.who: His painting Impression, Sunrise gave the Impressionist movement its name. He spent his last thirty years painting his own garden pond.
Claude Monet.goodAt: Light, and painting the same subject over and over to show how it changes.

Berthe Morisot.who: A founding member of the Impressionists who showed in all but one of their exhibitions. She was Manet's sister-in-law.
Berthe Morisot.goodAt: Fast, free brushwork and the private lives of women.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir.who: Started as a painter of porcelain, then became one of the best-loved Impressionists.
Pierre-Auguste Renoir.goodAt: Warm light, skin and happy social scenes.

Mary Cassatt.who: An American who moved to Paris and was invited by Degas to show with the Impressionists. She also persuaded American collectors to buy their work.
Mary Cassatt.goodAt: Mothers and children, painted without sentimentality, and printmaking influenced by Japanese art.

Gustave Caillebotte.who: A wealthy painter who also funded the Impressionist exhibitions and bought his friends' work. He left his collection to the French state.
Gustave Caillebotte.goodAt: The modern city, with dramatic perspective.

Paul Gauguin.from: Paris; later Brittany, Tahiti and the Marquesas
Paul Gauguin.who: A stockbroker who gave it up to paint. In Polynesia he took girls as young as 13 as 'wives', which is why many people now view his work critically.
Paul Gauguin.goodAt: Flat, bold colour and decorative design that shaped modern art.

Vincent van Gogh.from: Zundert, the Netherlands; worked in Paris and Arles, France
Vincent van Gogh.who: He painted about 860 oil paintings in roughly ten years and sold very few in his lifetime. His letters to his brother Theo are as famous as his art.
Vincent van Gogh.goodAt: Expressive colour and thick, energetic brushstrokes.

Cecilia Beaux.who: One of the most respected portrait painters in America, and the first woman to teach full time at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.
Cecilia Beaux.goodAt: Character, and confident handling of white paint.

John Singer Sargent.from: American, born in Florence, worked in London
John Singer Sargent.who: The most fashionable portrait painter of his day. His daring portrait Madame X caused such a scandal in Paris that he moved to London.
John Singer Sargent.goodAt: Dazzling, quick brushwork that turns into silk and lace from a distance.

Georges Seurat.who: He invented pointillism, painting in tiny dots of pure colour, and died at just 31.
Georges Seurat.goodAt: Colour theory and carefully designed compositions.

Henry Ossawa Tanner.who: The first African American painter to win international fame. He moved to Paris in 1891 partly to escape racism in America. His Banjo Lesson is a landmark.
Henry Ossawa Tanner.goodAt: Light, and religious scenes painted with real human feeling.

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec.from: Albi, southern France; worked in Montmartre, Paris
Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec.who: From an aristocratic family, he lived among the dancers and performers of Montmartre. His posters for the Moulin Rouge helped invent modern advertising.
Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec.goodAt: Expressive line, posters and nightlife characters.

Vasily Kandinsky.from: Moscow; worked in Munich, at the Bauhaus in Germany, and in Paris
Vasily Kandinsky.who: He gave up a career in law at 30 to paint, and became one of the pioneers of abstract art.
Vasily Kandinsky.goodAt: Abstraction. He believed colours could be heard like music.

Olowe of Ise.who: The best-known Yoruba sculptor of the twentieth century, working for kings across the region. His work is now in major museums worldwide.
Olowe of Ise.goodAt: Figures that seem to move and step out of the wood.

George Wesley Bellows.from: Ohio; worked in New York, USA
George Wesley Bellows.who: Linked to the Ashcan School, which painted real city life. Famous for his boxing paintings.

Unknown Mughal artist.who: Mughal emperors ran workshops where teams of painters made portraits and book illustrations. Many artists' names were not recorded.
Unknown Mughal artist.goodAt: Extraordinary fine detail, painted with brushes sometimes made of a single hair.
